title: He Knew the Betrayal Was Coming—And He Washed His Feet Anyway
paragraphs:
He Knew the Betrayal Was Coming—And He Washed His Feet Anyway
The Forgotten Shock of John 13 That Changes Everything About Grace, Forgiveness, and the Heart of Jesus
There are moments in Scripture so shocking that familiarity has robbed them of their power.
This is one of them.
Most believers know the scene.
The upper room.
The final meal.
The shadow of the cross drawing near.
A basin.
A towel.
The Son of God kneeling before His disciples.
Yet hidden inside this sacred moment is a detail so staggering that if we truly understood it, it would completely transform how we view grace, forgiveness, discipleship, and even our own failures.
Jesus washed Judas' feet.
Not after the betrayal.
Before it.
Not after repentance.
Before the kiss.
Before the soldiers.
Before the silver was fully spent.
Before the darkness unfolded.
Jesus knew exactly who Judas was.
And He washed his feet anyway.
Sit with that for a moment.
Because most of us struggle to be kind to people who merely annoy us.
Jesus lovingly served the man who would soon help orchestrate His execution.
That is not merely kindness.
That is divine love operating at a level the human heart struggles to comprehend.
John records the moment with remarkable precision:
"Jesus knew that the Father had put all things under His power, and that He had come from God and was returning to God." (John 13:3)
Notice what comes next.
Because Jesus knew who He was, He rose from supper.
Because Jesus knew where He came from, He took a towel.
Because Jesus knew where He was going, He knelt down.
The world believes power is demonstrated by making others serve you.
Jesus demonstrated that true power serves.
The Greek text says Jesus "tithemi" (τίθημι)—laid aside His garments.
The same word appears elsewhere regarding His life.
He laid down His robe.
Soon He would lay down His life.
The towel around His waist became a living prophecy of the cross.
Everything in this room points forward to Calvary.
Yet one figure remains seated among the disciples.
Judas.
The betrayer.
The one whose heart was already moving toward darkness.
John tells us:
"The devil had already put into the heart of Judas Iscariot, Simon's son, to betray Him." (John 13:2)
The Greek phrase is astonishing.
"Beblēkotos eis tēn kardian" (βεβληκότος εἰς τὴν καρδίαν).
Literally, something had been cast into the heart.
The seed of betrayal was already there.
Jesus knew it.
Nothing was hidden.
Nothing surprised Him.
Nothing caught heaven off guard.
Yet the basin remained full.
The towel remained in His hands.
And Judas remained included.
Imagine the silence.
One by one the disciples watched the Messiah kneel before them.
Dust-covered feet.
Calloused heels.
Road-worn skin.
Then Jesus arrived before Judas.
The room probably did not react.
The disciples did not yet understand.
But Jesus knew.
Judas knew.
And perhaps for a brief moment their eyes met.
The Creator touching the feet of the man preparing to sell Him.
The Savior serving the sinner.
The Holy One loving the traitor.
This is not weakness.
This is grace.
The Greek word for grace, charis (χάρις), is often defined as unearned favor.
But in Scripture it is much more than a theological concept.
Grace is God's goodness moving toward those who cannot deserve it.
Judas could not earn this act.
Yet Jesus gave it.
This reveals something profound about God's character.
Many people assume God's love exists only for those who are faithful.
But Scripture repeatedly shows God's love reaching people before they respond.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"While we were still sinners, Christ died for us."
Not after we improved.
Not after we cleaned ourselves up.
Not after we became worthy.
While we were still sinners.
Judas' feet are a living illustration of that truth.
Jesus was not discovering whether Judas would betray Him.
Jesus already knew.
And still He served.
Perhaps that is why this story unsettles us.
Because most of us prefer justice before mercy.
We want betrayal exposed before compassion offered.
We want consequences before kindness.
We want vindication before forgiveness.
Jesus reverses the order.
Not because betrayal is acceptable.
Not because sin is insignificant.
But because divine love does not wait for worthiness.
It initiates.
It pursues.
It reaches.
It kneels.
The Hebrew Scriptures had already foreshadowed this astonishing reality.
The prophet Isaiah wrote:
"He was despised and rejected by men." (Isaiah 53:3)
The Hebrew word translated "despised" is bazah (בָּזָה), meaning to regard as worthless, to reject, to treat with contempt.
Jesus willingly stepped into rejection.
Not accidentally.
Not reluctantly.
Intentionally.
The feet He washed would soon run away from Him.
The disciple He served would soon betray Him.
The crowds He healed would soon cry for His death.
And still He loved.
This is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because Judas is not merely a historical figure.
He represents every human heart that has chosen something over Christ.
Every compromise.
Every secret sin.
Every act of rebellion.
Every season of spiritual drift.
Every moment we have loved something more than God.
The uncomfortable truth is that we often read ourselves into the story as Peter.
But many times we resemble Judas more than we wish to admit.
And yet Jesus continues to pursue us.
Continues to call us.
Continues to extend grace.
Continues to offer mercy.
The tragedy of Judas was not merely his betrayal.
The tragedy was his refusal to return.
Peter denied Jesus three times.
Judas betrayed Him once.
Yet Peter ran toward grace.
Judas ran from it.
Both failed.
Only one surrendered.
This distinction matters.
Because no failure places someone beyond Christ's reach.
No scandal.
No addiction.
No divorce.
No shame.
No hidden struggle.
No collapse.
No past.
No wound.
No betrayal.
No sin.
The Gospel is not a story about good people becoming slightly better.
It is a story about dead people being made alive.
It is a story about rebels becoming sons and daughters.
It is a story about scandal becoming grace.
This is why the foot washing scene remains one of the most powerful portraits of the Gospel in all of Scripture.
Jesus knew the worst thing Judas would do.
And loved him to the very end.
John 13:1 says:
"Having loved His own who were in the world, He loved them to the end."
The Greek phrase is eis telos (εἰς τέλος).
It can mean completely.
Perfectly.
To the fullest extent.
To the uttermost.
Jesus loved Judas all the way to the edge of betrayal.
And He loves us all the way to the edge of our brokenness too.
Perhaps someone reading this feels unworthy of God's grace.
Perhaps you carry memories you cannot escape.
Mistakes you cannot undo.
Regrets that revisit you at night.
Failures that still whisper accusations.
The basin in the upper room tells a different story.
The towel tells a different story.
The cross tells a different story.
Jesus already knew everything about you.
And He went to Calvary anyway.
That is the Gospel.
Not that you are good enough.
But that Christ is gracious enough.
Not that you deserve forgiveness.
But that He delights in giving it.
Not that your story is finished.
But that Jesus rewrites stories.
That truth is at the very heart of our mission.
Every article we publish, every resource we create, every testimony we share exists for one purpose: helping people encounter the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.

You never know who is silently carrying shame, wrestling with betrayal, or wondering whether God could still love them. One share may place hope directly in the path of someone who desperately needs it.
Before you leave, be honest.
Has there been a place in your life where you assumed God's grace could not reach?
Your testimony may encourage someone else to return to Christ today.
Because the hands that washed Judas' feet are the same hands that were pierced for your redemption.
And that changes everything.
The basin was never about clean feet.
It was always about a Savior who loved sinners before they ever loved Him back.
